notes.meaning: Asher's border swung eastward toward Beth-dagon and touched the land of Zebulun before turning north past Cabul. In ancient Hebrew thinking, directions were taken while facing the sunrise, so the left side meant the north. The town name Beth-dagon shows that shrines to the fish-god Dagon were scattered across northern Canaan long before Israel arrived.

The border ran through several northern towns and reached out toward the Phoenician port of Greater Sidon. Sidon was an ancient, wealthy trade city on the Mediterranean coast. Although this territory was marked out for Asher, Israel never conquered or occupied Sidon itself.

The line turned southward toward the fortified city of Tyre and came out at the Mediterranean Sea near Achzib. This city of Tyre was the old walled settlement on the mainland, long before the famous island fortress was built. Many Canaanite refugees took shelter in heavily defended harbors like Tyre and Sidon as Joshua's armies advanced.

Asher received twenty-two cities along with their surrounding country villages. The earlier list names extra towns because it includes border posts belonging to neighboring tribes. Aphek later became known as the site where Israel's King Ahab defeated the Syrian army of Ben-hadad.

The sixth lot was drawn for the families of the tribe of Naphtali. Jacob had once described Naphtali as a free deer that speaks pleasant words, picturing a peaceful and fruitful people. Their homeland was placed in the far north of Canaan near the hills of Lebanon.

Naphtali's northern boundary began near an oak grove at Zaanannim and ran eastward to the Jordan River. The oak trees stood near Kedesh, marking a recognizable natural point in the landscape. The upper Jordan River and its northern lakes formed the natural eastern edge of the tribe's land.

The boundary turned west toward Mount Tabor, bordering Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west. The phrase mentioning Judah on the eastern side points to towns across the Jordan held by Jair, whose family tree went back to Judah. The river also served as a water route linking northern families with their southern brothers.

Naphtali was given strong, walled towns around the Sea of Galilee, which was then called Chinnereth. Hammath was famous for its natural hot springs, and Chinnereth gave its name to both the rich lakeside plain and the lake itself. Hazor was the ancient royal city that Joshua had previously burned during the northern conquest.

This list completes the nineteen fortified towns set within Naphtali's territory. Kedesh later became a city of refuge, a safe place where someone who caused an accidental death could flee from revenge. The tribe did not immediately drive out every Canaanite population, leaving places like Beth-anath to be subdued later.

This summary closes the description of Naphtali's inheritance and rural settlements. Naphtali received one of the most beautiful and fertile areas in all of Canaan. Centuries later, Jesus carried out much of his public preaching and healing in this very region around the Sea of Galilee.

The seventh and final lot fell to the families of the tribe of Dan. Even though Dan led a large division of troops through the wilderness, they waited until the very end to receive their portion. God placed them in a challenging spot between Judah and the Mediterranean coast.

Dan's territory was carved out of land previously given to Judah and Ephraim. Towns like Zorah and Eshtaol became famous as the home district of the judge Samson. Ekron was a powerful Philistine center, which meant the Danites had dangerous neighbors right beside them.

Dan's border reached out to the coastline near Joppa, the primary natural seaport of ancient Israel. Several of these towns, such as Eltekeh and Gath-rimmon, were later given to the Levites as places to live. Although the coastal plain was fertile and attractive, Dan struggled to hold it against entrenched Philistines and Amorites.

Fierce neighbors pushed the Danites into the hills, so their original territory became too cramped to live in. Later in their history, a group of Danite warriors marched to the far northern edge of the land, captured the city of Leshem, and renamed it Dan. This northern outpost created the famous boundary saying 'from Dan to Beersheba' to describe the whole nation from top to bottom.

This verse concludes the record of Dan's tribal inheritance and surrounding villages. The capture of northern Leshem was recorded here so readers could see all the lands of Dan in a single account. It shows how Dan's people ended up living both along the central coast and in the distant north.

Joshua did not ask for any personal property until every single tribe had received its land. Even though he was Israel's highest leader, he refused to use his authority for private gain. By putting the people's needs before his own comfort, Joshua showed true humility and servant leadership.

Joshua asked for Timnath-serah, a rugged, ruined town in the hill country of his own tribe of Ephraim. The Lord had promised him an inheritance just as He had promised Caleb, and the people gladly granted his request. Instead of choosing a rich estate, Joshua was content to rebuild a broken town and settle there.

This formal summary brings the distribution of the Promised Land to a close. Eleazar the high priest, Joshua, and the tribal chiefs drew the lots publicly at Shiloh before the Lord's sacred tent. Because God Himself guided every choice, the tribes accepted their portions with peace and gratitude.
